summary: This standards-track document defines more identifier type numbers for the mobile node identifier option in Mobile IPv6, which RFC 4283 introduced. The new types let a mobile node be identified in additional ways.

eli5.summary: A phone needs a name tag. This adds new kinds of name tags so networks can recognize traveling devices in more ways.

subtitle: New kinds of identifier, such as IMSI, MAC addresses and DUIDs, for naming a mobile node in Mobile IPv6.

tldr.problem: The Mobile Node Identifier option for Mobile IPv6 had only one identifier type, the NAI, even though other identifiers are in common use for authenticating mobile nodes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers further identifier type numbers (IPv6 address, IMSI, P-TMSI, EUI-48, EUI-64, GUTI and DUID) and says how the IPv6, IMSI, EUI and DUID types are encoded.
tldr.outcome: Deployments can identify a device by an identifier it already has, with signaling that carries these identifiers required to be encrypted.

today: RFC 8371 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the option defined in RFC 4283.

sections.title: Why More Identifier Types
sections.content:
The Mobile Node Identifier Option for Mobile IPv6 (RFC 4283) has been a popular way to give mobile nodes an identifier during authentication with AAA protocols such as Diameter. Until this RFC only one type had been specified, the Mobile Node (MN) NAI.

Other identifiers are in common use. Identifiers tied to the physical device, such as the MAC address, help deployment because they are often the most natural way to identify the device and avoid extra lookup steps.
sections.eli5: Until now there was only one kind of name tag. Networks already use other ones, so this adds them to the list.

sections.title: The New Identifier Types
sections.content:
Table 1 of the RFC lists the new types and where each is defined: the IPv6 address (RFC 4291), IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity), P-TMSI (Packet - Temporary Mobile Subscriber Identity) and GUTI (Globally Unique Temporary UE Identity), all from 3GPP, the EUI-48 and EUI-64 IEEE addresses, and the DUID (DHCPv6 Unique Identifier, RFC 3315).

The RFC only describes encoding for some of them in Section 4; for the 3GPP temporary identifiers it points to the 3GPP specification for details of the format.
sections.eli5: The list now includes things like the number on a SIM card, the serial number of a network chip, and a temporary visitor badge number.

sections.title: How Each Type Is Encoded
sections.content:
The IPv6 address is a 16-octet string holding a full address assigned to the node. It MUST be a unicast routable address; multicast, link-local and the unspecified address MUST NOT be used. Unique Local Addresses MAY be used if any security operation using them takes into account the domain in which the ULA is unique.

The IMSI is at most 15 decimal digits, encoded in network order with 4 bits per digit. If needed to fill the last octet, the last digit MUST be padded with 0xf. The RFC's example IMSI 123456123456789 becomes 0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78, 0x9f.

An EUI-48 address is encoded as 6 octets and an EUI-64 address as 8 octets. A DUID has several types distinguished by an initial two-octet type field; clients and servers MUST treat DUIDs as opaque values and MUST only compare them for equality.
sections.eli5: Each kind of name tag has its own way of being written into bytes. A SIM-card number is written two digits to a byte, with a filler at the end if the count is odd.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
The RFC adds no security mechanism and does not affect existing ones. It treats these identifiers as private information: if used in the MN identifier extension of RFC 4283, the packet including it MUST be encrypted so that no personal information or trackable identifiers are disclosed to passive observers. Operators can potentially use IPsec ESP in transport mode with confidentiality and integrity protection.

Some of these identifiers are used in other standards bodies' protocols only during initial network entry, after which a temporary identifier is used. Managing the link between long-lived and temporary identifiers is outside the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: A name tag can be used to follow you around, so messages carrying it have to be sealed in an envelope that outsiders cannot read.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The new types were assigned numbers in the Mobile Node Identifier Option Subtypes registry. Numbers 9 to 15 are Reserved and 16 to 255 are Unassigned. The registration procedure is Standards Action (RFC 8126), and the expert must ascertain that a new type allows unique identification of the mobile device.
sections.eli5: Each new name tag type got its own number in an official list, and some numbers are kept free for later.

sections.title: Appendix: RFID Types
sections.content:
A non-normative appendix lists RFID identifier types that were originally meant for the main body but were moved because there was insufficient support at the time. It notes that RFID-based mobile devices may create privacy exposures unless signaling is confidential.

The appendix describes the TRACK-IoT project's exploration of Mobile IPv6 for RFID-based devices, with examples such as tracking cold food or pieces of art in transport. It then lists 64-bit, 96-bit and URI forms of EPC schemes such as SGTIN, SSCC, SGLN, GRAI and GIAI, plus a US Department of Defense construct, and refers to the EPC Tag Data Standard for details. No type numbers are assigned to them in this document.
sections.eli5: The back of the document talks about using the tags on shipping boxes as name tags too, but it is only an idea and gets no official numbers.
